content: Asphalt, also known as bitumen outside North America, is a sticky, black, and highly viscous liquid or semi-solid material. It is found in most crude petroleum and some natural deposits, where it is sometimes referred to as asphaltum. Chemically, asphalt is often modeled as a colloid, with asphaltenes forming the dispersed phase and maltenes constituting the continuous phase, though there is some debate among chemists regarding its precise structure. In technical terminology, asphalt (or asphalt cement) refers to the carefully refined residue obtained from the distillation of selected crude oils. Outside North America, this product is commonly called bitumen. The primary application of asphalt (bitumen) is in road construction, where it serves as a binder or adhesive for aggregate particles. The resulting road surface material is typically referred to as asphalt concrete in North America or simply asphalt elsewhere. However, the interchangeable use of the terms asphalt and bitumen often leads to confusion outside the road construction industry, despite clear definitions within the field. Asphalt is sometimes confused with tar, a similar black thermoplastic material produced through the destructive distillation of coal. During the early and mid-20th century, when town gas was widely produced, tar was readily available and extensively used as a binder for road aggregates. The addition of tar to macadam roads gave rise to the term tarmac, which is now commonly used to describe road-making materials. However, since the 1970s, with the advent of natural gas replacing town gas, asphalt (bitumen) has largely replaced tar in these applications. Asphalt is separated from other components in crude oil, such as naphtha, gasoline, and diesel, through fractional distillation, often conducted under vacuum conditions. Further separation can be achieved by processing the heavier fractions of crude oil in a de-asphalting unit, which uses supercritical propane or butane to dissolve lighter molecules, which are then separated. Additional processing, such as blowing the product with oxygen, can make the asphalt harder and more viscous. Natural deposits of asphalt include lake asphalts, such as those from Pitch Lake in Trinidad and Tobago and Bermudez Lake in Venezuela, as well as Gilsonite, the Dead Sea between Israel and Jordan, and tar sands. Asphalt is typically stored and transported at temperatures around 150 degrees Celsius (300°F). To maintain its liquidity during shipping, diesel oil or kerosene is sometimes mixed in, but these lighter materials are separated upon delivery. This mixture is often referred to as bitumen feedstock (BFS). Some dump trucks route hot engine exhaust through pipes in the dump body to keep the material warm. Additionally, the backs of tippers carrying asphalt and some handling equipment are commonly sprayed with a releasing agent before filling to facilitate material release. Diesel oil is sometimes used as a releasing agent, though it can mix with and degrade the quality of the asphalt. In ancient times, natural asphalt deposits were used in the Middle East as mortar between bricks and stones, for ship caulking, and for waterproofing. The Persian word for asphalt, mumiya, may be related to the English word mummy, as asphalt was also used by ancient Egyptians for embalming mummies. In the ancient Far East, natural asphalt was slowly boiled to remove lighter fractions, leaving a thermoplastic material of higher molecular weight that hardened upon cooling. This was used to coat scabbards and other objects requiring waterproofing. The largest use of asphalt today is in the production of asphalt concrete for road surfaces, accounting for approximately 80% of asphalt consumption in the United States. Roofing shingles represent most of the remaining asphalt usage. Other applications include cattle sprays, fence post treatments, and fabric waterproofing. Asphalt road surfaces are the most widely recycled material in the U.S., both by gross tonnage and percentage. According to a report by the Federal Highway Administration and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 80% of the asphalt removed annually during road widening and resurfacing projects is reused in new roads, roadbeds, shoulders, and embankments. Mastic asphalt is a type of asphalt with a higher bitumen (binder) content, typically around 7-10% of the aggregate mix, compared to roller asphalt, which contains about 5% added bitumen. Stone mastic asphalt (SMA) is another type of asphalt gaining global popularity due to its high anti-skid properties, resulting from its high aggregate density and minimal void content. SMA also offers greater durability compared to alternative road asphalt surfaces. However, improper manufacturing or application can lead to slippery road surfaces due to excess bitumen pooling (bleeding) on the surface. Asphalt emulsions allow for mixing at much lower temperatures. These involve combining asphalt with petroleum solvents to form cutbacks with reduced melting points or mixing with water to create an emulsion. Emulsions are categorized as cationic or anionic, depending on their affinity for aggregates. Asphalt emulsions are used in various applications, such as chip seal, where the road surface is sprayed with asphalt emulsion followed by a layer of crushed rock or gravel, and slurry seal, which involves spreading a mixture of asphalt emulsion and fine crushed aggregate on a road surface. Cold-mixed asphalt can also be made from asphalt emulsion to create pavements similar to hot-mixed asphalt, several inches in depth. Emulsions are also blended into recycled hot-mix asphalt to produce low-cost pavements. Asphalt can sometimes be mixed with petroleum-contaminated soil, such as the output from low-temperature thermal desorption processes. In response to growing concerns about global climate change and pollution from fossil fuel combustion, environmentally friendly and non-toxic alternatives to bitumen have been developed. Bitumen can now be produced from non-petroleum-based renewable resources, such as sugar, molasses, rice, corn, and potato starches. Additionally, bitumen can be made from waste material, such as vacuum tower bottoms produced during the cleaning of used motor oils, which supports recycling industries. These waste materials are typically disposed of by burning or dumping in landfills. Non-petroleum-based bitumen binders can also be pigmented, reducing road surface temperatures and mitigating the urban heat island effect, which contributes to global climate change. Urban heat islands, where urban and suburban temperatures are 2 to 10°F (1 to 6°C) higher than nearby rural areas, are a growing concern for millions of people living in and around cities. Elevated temperatures increase peak energy demand, air conditioning costs, air pollution levels, and heat-related illnesses and mortality. Communities can mitigate these effects by replacing conventional black asphalt road surfaces with new pigmentable bitumen that produces lighter colors. Asphalt made with vegetable oil-based binders was patented by Colas SA in France in 2004 under the name Vegecol. Colas was originally owned by Royal Dutch Shell. Some homeowners seeking environmentally friendly alternatives to asphalt for paving have experimented with waste vegetable oil as a binder for driveways and parking areas. The earliest known test occurred in 2002 in Ohio, where a homeowner combined waste vegetable oil with dry aggregate to create a low-cost, non-polluting paving material for a 200-foot driveway. After five years, the homeowner reported that the driveway performed as well as or better than petroleum-based materials. This movement led Shell Oil Company to pave two public roads in Norway in 2007 with Colas vegetable-oil-based asphalt. Results of this study are still pending. The word asphalt is derived from late Middle English, originating from the French word asphalte, which is based on the late Latin asphaltum and the Greek asphaltos (ἄσφαλτος), meaning to make firm or to secure.
